newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany, Italy play down speculation of EMU rift.
newsitem.headline: Germany, Italy play down speculation of EMU rift.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi played down speculation on Friday of a rift over whether Italy can be among the first nations to adopt Europe's single currency.
"There are essentially no areas in which bilateral difficulties come into question and we are both on the way to build Europe," Kohl told a news conference after a one-day meeting with Prodi.
Prodi, echoing Kohl's comments, said he had no doubts about Italy's excellent relations with Germany and predicted Italy was well on course to be among the first entrants.
"Italy would be far enough along to allow this next year," Prodi said. But he added that "time will be the final judge" about the euro's first members.
The two leaders discussed Italy's efforts to join the single European currency, which is set to begin in 1999.

The summit came after a report in Britain's Financial Times newspaper earlier this week that European Union and central bank officials were discussing a plan to defer Italian entry into the currency, in part to assuage German fears of a soft euro.
But Kohl said Germany would not participate in making judgements on who will join currency union a year before the decision needs to be taken, describing such speculation as "unacceptable".
He noted Germany itself had much work ahead and would make all efforts to stick to all of the criteria that must be met for Economic and Monetary Union.

"We want to meet the deadline and we also want to meet the criteria," he said, adding however that Germany could miss fulfilling Maastricht Treaty criteria without taking what he described as "political measures".
Kohl in particular highlighted Germany's chronically high unemployment levels as one area that it needed to address immediately.
"We are looking at developments which should lead to an improvement in the employment situation by the middle of 1997," he said.
Figures released on Thursday the jobless rate in Germany reached a post-war record of 12.2 percent, with an unadjusted total of 4.658 million people out of work.
Kohl said the unemployment rate in Germany, like that in Italy, was "completely unacceptable".
He noted however that he had been widely misquoted in media reports as saying that he expected to half German jobless levels by the turn of the century.
He said the halving of unemployment was not a forecast but "a goal" and one that he was continuing to aim at.
